title: round(2.5) is 2 in Python but Math.round(2.5) is 3 in JavaScript
assumption: Rounding a value that is exactly halfway between two integers always rounds up, in every language.

input.display: round(2.5) in Python 3 vs Math.round(2.5) in JavaScript, and round(-2.5) vs Math.round(-2.5)
input.description: A genuine tie - e.g. rounding a $2.50 half-unit quantity, or a tax amount that lands exactly on a half-cent after an earlier exact calculation - rounded to the nearest whole unit.

what_goes_wrong: The exact same halfway value rounds to a different integer depending on the language: Python's round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4 (always to the nearest even integer), while JavaScript's Math.round(2.5) is 3 (always rounds .5 up, toward positive infinity) - and Math.round(-2.5) is -2, not -3, because "up" for Math.round means toward +Infinity even on the negative side.
why: Python 3's round() implements round-half-to-even ("banker's rounding", IEEE 754's default rounding mode) specifically to avoid statistical bias from always rounding .5 the same direction over many values. JavaScript's Math.round() is specified (ECMA-262) to round half-way cases toward +Infinity, not away from zero and not to even - which is why -2.5 rounds to -2 (toward +Infinity means less negative) rather than -3. Neither behavior is a bug; they are different, deliberately documented rounding rules, and porting rounding logic between the two languages without accounting for the difference changes answers for every exact half.
fix: Decide and document one rounding rule for money (customer-facing amounts commonly use round-half-up, away from zero; some accounting contexts deliberately use half-even) and implement it explicitly - e.g. Python's decimal.Decimal.quantize(..., rounding=decimal.ROUND_HALF_UP) - rather than relying on whatever a language's built-in round happens to do.

test_cases.note: A cross-language rounding function should not assume their_function(2.5) gives the same result as Math.round(2.5) in JS (3) or round(2.5) in Python (2) by default - pick one explicit rule and implement it the same way everywhere.
